source.title: Emergence in non-neural models: grokking modular arithmetic via average gradient outer product
source.authors: Neil Rohit Mallinar; Daniel Beaglehole; Libin Zhu; Adityanarayanan Radhakrishnan; Parthe Pandit; M. Belkin

record.tranche_reason: The study reproduces delayed train/test accuracy separation on modular arithmetic with neural networks and tests the same behavior using iterative kernel-RFM models.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own accuracy trajectories, feature-progress measures, and regularization comparisons. Results from prior work are cited but are not recorded as rows. It also reports fixed random-feature and imposed-circulant experiments, which concern feature structure and generalization but do not measure gradual formation of a circuit.
record.test_reason: The study reproduces grokking in one-hidden-layer quadratic networks on modular arithmetic (p=61), using the same train/test accuracy trajectory measure as the originals. It also shows the same delayed jump in non-neural kernel-RFM, and tracks continuous progress measures (circulant deviation, AGOP alignment) that improve before the jump. The RFM and regularization results also carry a specific argument against weight-norm and circuit-efficiency explanations (V5).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that grokking of modular arithmetic occurs in non-neural, non-gradient kernel-RFM as well as in networks, and is fully determined by gradual learning of block-circulant features. Neither training nor test loss predicts the jump. They add that their progress measures are a posteriori, that kernels with such features implement the Fourier Multiplication Algorithm, and that lazy-to-rich or circuit-efficiency explanations cannot be general.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the modular-arithmetic train/test accuracy trajectory, but adds AGOP-based kernel-RFM and uses one-hidden-layer quadratic networks; the paper does not claim an explicit replication of the original study's full setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports different grokking behavior with and without regularization, and faster generalization with random block-circulant input maps or imposed block-circulant feature structure. It does not report a sweep of the training-set-size effect on optimization delay.

fits_no_version.finding: Fixed random block-circulant input maps, or imposed circulant feature structure, let kernels and networks generalize and accelerate grokking.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A generic block-circulant feature structure is sufficient for generalization on modular arithmetic; supplying it removes most of the delay.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed 30 iterations, test accuracy changes sharply with training fraction while test loss and AGOP alignment change gradually.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Emergence with respect to data size may be a metric artifact, unlike emergence with respect to compute.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report no lazy-to-rich two-phase transition: RFM and network features improve from early training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking can occur without a lazy-to-rich transition, so that transition is not a general explanation of grokking.

record.problems: Many trajectory values are presented only in figures, without exact numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The training-fraction experiment evaluates after a fixed number of iterations and does not test how the delay changes with dataset size. The proposed progress measures require final-model information or knowledge of the circulant structure.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were left out.

untested.parts: Whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks. The data-fraction sweep (App. Fig. 6) is at a fixed iteration count.

Later removal of memorizing components. Empirical tracking of a Fourier circuit forming in networks: the FMA link is a theorem for kernels with a constructed feature matrix, not measured during training.
Non-algorithmic data, and switching grokking via initialization scale or weight norm. The authors only argue that grokking occurs without a lazy-to-rich phase.
Circuit efficiency, critical dataset size, and ungrokking below it.
Comparison of algorithms across runs, architectures or hyperparameters. The study only notes that RFM and networks both learn block-circulant features.
No control of optimizer or numerical artifacts. RFM groks with no gradient-based optimizer, but this is not a test of the artifact account.

missing.what: Test loss of the correct output class tracks total test loss and also transitions sharply, so the averaged loss is not hiding gradual progress
missing.locator: Section 3 and Fig. 2A third row; Section 4 and Fig. 5A third row

missing.what: Pearson correlations between the network's NFM and the square root of its AGOP: 0.955/0.942/0.924/0.929 (add/sub/mul/div)
Explicit argument that circuit-efficiency and weight-magnitude explanations cannot account for grokking in RFM

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V1 limits_scope label on R35-R36 was dropped: those rows are not linked to V1, and the dataset-size dependence of the delay is untested rather than qualified. The network experiments use strong weight decay (1.0), which the rows omit. In V2, the theorem linking circulant features to the FMA is a construction with per-class feature matrices, not evidence of the learned circuit. The suggestion that RFM and networks find similar algorithms touches V6 only loosely and was not labelled. The paper is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks during optimization.

It measures gradual progress in AGOP alignment and circulant structure, but does not track memorizing components being removed later. The FMA result is theoretical for kernel machines, not a direct identification of the neural network circuit.
No non-algorithmic image, text, or molecule tasks are tested; no initialization-scale or lazy-to-rich intervention is tested.
No realistic large-model pretraining or fine-tuning is tested.
The study compares regularization effects on grokking but does not measure circuit efficiency, a critical dataset-size prediction, or ungrokking below a dataset-size threshold.
It does not compare identifiable algorithms across independent runs, architectures, or hyperparameters.
No adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point/softmax artifact control is tested.
